ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A and B are the sources of two waves. At $\mathtt{t}=0$, both sources simultaneously start to perform simple harmonic motion perpendicular to the plane of the paper. Their vibration expressions are $\mathtt{x}_{\mathrm{A}}{=}0.1\sin（2πt）\mathbf{m}$ and $\mathtt{x}_{\mathrm{B}}{=}0.5\sin（2πt）\mathbf{m}$, respectively. The two waves generated propagate along the plane of the paper in the same homogeneous medium. P is a point in the medium that starts to vibrate at $\mathbf{t}=2\mathbf{s}$. It is known that $\mathrm{PA}{=}40\mathrm{cm}$ and $\mathrm{PB}{=}50\mathrm{cm}$.

1. Find the wave speed of two waves.
2. The distance traveled by particle P in $\mathrm{t}=4.25\mathrm{s}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there are two wave sources A and B; A is located at the upper left, B is located at the lower left, and the observation point P is located at the lower right. In the figure, dashed lines mark the oblique propagation path AP from A to P, and the nearly horizontal propagation path BP from B to P, indicating that the two waves propagate from A and B to P respectively. Reasoning: From the problem, PA = 40 cm = 0.40 m, PB = 50 cm = 0.50 m. The two wave sources A and B begin vibrating simultaneously at t = 0, while P begins vibrating only at t = 2 s. Since AP is shorter, the disturbance that first reaches P comes from A, so the wave speed v = PA / 2 s = 0.40 / 2 = 0.20 m/s. The vibration expressions of the two wave sources both contain sin(2πt), so the period T = 1 s. The time for wave B to reach P is PB / v = 0.50 / 0.20 = 2.5 s. Therefore: from t = 0 to 2 s, P does not vibrate, and the distance traveled is 0; from t = 2 s to 2.5 s, only wave A makes P vibrate, lasting 0.5 s = T/2, with amplitude 0.1 m, and the distance traveled by the particle is 2A = 2 × 0.1 = 0.2 m. After t = 2.5 s, both waves have reached P. The wavelength λ = vT = 0.20 × 1 = 0.20 m. The path difference PB - PA = 0.50 - 0.40 = 0.10 m = λ/2, so the phase difference of the two waves at P is π, and they superpose in opposite phase. The resultant amplitude is |0.5 - 0.1| = 0.4 m. From t = 2.5 s to t = 4.25 s, the duration is 1.75 s = 7T/4, that is, 7 quarter-periods. In each quarter-period, the distance passed through by the particle equals the resultant amplitude 0.4 m, so the distance for this interval is 7 × 0.4 = 2.8 m. The total distance is 0.2 + 2.8 = 3.0 m.

method.method_draft: Use a chronological arrival-time timeline. First read from the diagram that A and B are two separated point sources and P is the observation point, with dashed paths AP and BP indicating the two propagation distances. From the text, use PA = 40 cm, PB = 50 cm, the sources start together at t = 0, and P first starts vibrating at t = 2 s. Since AP is the shorter path, the first disturbance to reach P is from A, so v = 0.40 m / 2 s = 0.20 m/s. The source period is T = 1 s from sin(2πt). Thus the A wave reaches P at t = 2 s and the B wave reaches P at t = 0.50/0.20 = 2.5 s. From t = 2 to 2.5 s, P executes half a cycle with amplitude 0.1 m, so the traveled distance is 2A = 0.2 m. After t = 2.5 s, both waves act. The path difference is 0.10 m, and λ = vT = 0.20 m, so the phase difference is π; the resultant amplitude is |0.5 - 0.1| = 0.4 m. From t = 2.5 to 4.25 s is 1.75 s = 7 quarter-periods, so the particle travels 7 × 0.4 = 2.8 m. Add the earlier 0.2 m to get 3.0 m.

method.method_draft: Write explicit delayed wave functions at P and integrate the absolute velocity piecewise. From the diagram, identify that P receives one wave along AP and one along BP. From the text, convert PA = 0.40 m and PB = 0.50 m. Because P begins to vibrate at t = 2 s and AP is the nearer path, set v = 0.40/2 = 0.20 m/s. The delayed displacement from A at P is y_A(t) = 0.1 sin[2π(t - 2)] for t ≥ 2. The delayed displacement from B is y_B(t) = 0.5 sin[2π(t - 2.5)] for t ≥ 2.5. For 2 ≤ t < 2.5, y = y_A. The traveled distance is ∫_2^2.5 |dy_A/dt| dt, giving 0.2 m. For 2.5 ≤ t ≤ 4.25, add the displacements: y = 0.1 sin[2π(t - 2)] + 0.5 sin[2π(t - 2.5)] = -0.4 sin[2π(t - 2)], so |dy/dt| is that of SHM with amplitude 0.4 m. Integrate |dy/dt| over 1.75 periods-worth of time, or equivalently over seven quarter-cycles, to obtain 2.8 m. Total distance is 3.0 m.

推理：先把距离化为国际单位：PA = 0.40 m，PB = 0.50 m。P 在 t = 2 s 开始振动，最先到达 P 的应是较短路径 AP 上由 A 发出的波，所以波速 v = PA / 2 = 0.40 / 2 = 0.20 m/s。

B 发出的波到达 P 的时间为 PB / v = 0.50 / 0.20 = 2.5 s。因此 P 处的延迟振动为：当 t ≥ 2 时，y_A(t) = 0.1 sin[2π(t - 2)]；当 t ≥ 2.5 时，y_B(t) = 0.5 sin[2π(t - 2.5)]。

总路程为 0.2 + 2.8 = 3.0 m。

raw_record.original_question:
A and B are the sources of two waves. At $t=0$, both sources simultaneously start to perform simple harmonic motion perpendicular to the plane of the paper. Their vibration expressions are $x_A=0.1\sin(2\pi t)\,\mathrm{m}$ and $x_B=0.5\sin(2\pi t)\,\mathrm{m}$, respectively. The two waves generated propagate along the plane of the paper in the same homogeneous medium. P is a point in the medium that starts to vibrate at $t=2\,\mathrm{s}$. It is known that $PA=40\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $PB=50\,\mathrm{cm}$.

1. Find the wave speed of the two waves.
2. Find the distance traveled by particle P in $t=4.25\,\mathrm{s}$.
raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: In the figure there are two wave sources A and B; A is located at the upper left, B is located at the lower left, and the observation point P is located at the lower right. In the figure, dashed lines mark the oblique propagation path AP from A to P, and the nearly horizontal propagation path BP from B to P, indicating that the two waves propagate from A and B to P respectively.

Reasoning: From the problem, PA = 40 cm = 0.40 m, PB = 50 cm = 0.50 m. The two wave sources A and B begin vibrating simultaneously at t = 0, while P begins vibrating only at t = 2 s. Since AP is shorter, the disturbance that first reaches P comes from A, so the wave speed v = PA / 2 s = 0.40 / 2 = 0.20 m/s.

The vibration expressions of the two wave sources both contain sin(2πt), so the period T = 1 s. The time for wave B to reach P is PB / v = 0.50 / 0.20 = 2.5 s. Therefore: from t = 0 to 2 s, P does not vibrate, and the distance traveled is 0; from t = 2 s to 2.5 s, only wave A makes P vibrate, lasting 0.5 s = T/2, with amplitude 0.1 m, and the distance traveled by the particle is 2A = 2 × 0.1 = 0.2 m.

After t = 2.5 s, both waves have reached P. The wavelength λ = vT = 0.20 × 1 = 0.20 m. The path difference PB - PA = 0.50 - 0.40 = 0.10 m = λ/2, so the phase difference of the two waves at P is π, and they superpose in opposite phase. The resultant amplitude is |0.5 - 0.1| = 0.4 m. From t = 2.5 s to t = 4.25 s, the duration is 1.75 s = 7T/4, that is, 7 quarter-periods. In each quarter-period, the distance passed through by the particle equals the resultant amplitude 0.4 m, so the distance for this interval is 7 × 0.4 = 2.8 m. The total distance is 0.2 + 2.8 = 3.0 m.
